match.reason: The bank point only introduces operations management in general terms and does not teach lean management, its tools such as pull production, one-piece flow, takt time and zero defects, or the idea of cutting non-value-adding steps.

draft.title: Lean management
card: Lean management cuts any step in operations that adds no value for the customer. Waste can be time, materials, movement or stock that sits unused.
Pull production
work starts only when a customer order or demand signals it. Goods are not made in advance on a guess.
One-piece flow
each item moves through the steps one at a time, not in large batches. Faults show up sooner.
Takt time and zero defects
takt time is the pace needed to meet demand, so one unit every two minutes means a takt time of two minutes. Zero defects is the goal of getting every item right first time.
draft.remember: Lean asks of every step: does it add value for the customer? If not, cut it.

a.q: Which feature of lean management means a bakery bakes loaves only after orders arrive from its cafe customers?
a.why: Pull production starts work only when demand signals it, so the bakery does not make loaves on a guess. One-piece flow is about moving items singly through steps, not about when work starts.
a.clue: Think about what triggers the work to begin.

b.q: Dev's workshop in Ballarat builds bikes. He changes from making frames in batches of 50 to passing each frame to the next step as soon as it is done. A faulty weld is now found within minutes. Which lean feature does this show?
b.why: Moving each item through the steps singly, not in batches, is one-piece flow, and it shows faults quickly. Zero defects is the goal of no faults, but the change described is how items move, not the goal.
b.clue: Look at how the frames move, not at the goal.

problems.detail: The takt time example ('one unit every two minutes means a takt time of two minutes') does not show where the pace comes from: available time divided by customer demand. Students could mistake takt time for the rate a line actually produces at (cycle time). A worked example would fix this, such as 240 units demanded in a 480-minute shift giving a takt time of two minutes.

check.summary: Both questions are sound, with one clear right answer each (pull production, one-piece flow). The only issue is that the card's takt time example does not link the pace to demand and available time, so students could confuse it with cycle time.

proposal.title: Lean management
card: Lean management cuts any step in operations that adds no value for the customer, such as waiting, extra movement or unused stock. It aims for zero defects: every item right first time.
Pull production
work starts only when a customer order or demand signals it. Goods are not made in advance on a guess.
One-piece flow
each item moves through the steps one at a time, not in large batches. Faults show up sooner.
Takt time
the pace that customer demand sets: available time ÷ units demanded. If 240 units are wanted in a 480-minute shift, takt time is two minutes per unit.
proposal.remember: Lean asks of every step: does it add value for the customer? If not, cut it.
